notes.prov-akwata-mpola: A real French proverb too: Qui va lentement va loin.
notes.prov-kamu-kamu: A fagot is a bundle of sticks. French also says Petit à petit, l’oiseau fait son nid.
notes.prov-agali-awamu: Same idea as L’union fait la force.
notes.haba-na-haba: French: Petit à petit, l’oiseau fait son nid.

guidebook.intro: Learn well-known Ganda and Swahili proverbs and how to use them. French proverbs often start with “qui” (whoever) and speak in the present.

tips.title: Qui va lentement va loin
body: Many French proverbs use **qui** for “whoever”: **Qui va lentement va loin** (whoever goes slowly goes far). **Qui n’écoute pas les anciens se casse la jambe.**

French has its own versions of some you’ll meet: **Petit à petit, l’oiseau fait son nid** (little by little the bird builds its nest), close to **Haba na haba**. **L’union fait la force** (unity is strength) is Belgium’s motto and the meaning of **Agali awamu**.

tips.title: Comme on dit
body: Introduce a proverb with **Comme on dit…** (as they say) and explain it with **Ça veut dire que…** (it means that…).
**On** is the general “people, they, you”: **On dit que…** (people say that…).

culture.title: Proverbs in conversation
body: Across francophone Africa, elders end discussions with a proverb, and quoting one well shows respect for tradition. Many local proverbs have been translated into French and are used in speeches and newspapers.
